purpose: Corrected reviews for staging cross-reference entries whose reading was mapped to the wrong Greek verse or wrongly reported as unavailable. One record per chapter, in the saints-xref-review format, keyed by data-sxe-edge. Each review also carries corrected_reading (the Saints anchor the entry should display), which the importer must apply for the review to be valid.

1-corinthians-11:2:2.summary: 1 Corinthians 11:2 has Paul say, “I praise you because you remember me”; Proverbs 31:28–31 tells how “her husband praised her.” Only the word “praise” is shared.
1-corinthians-11:2:2.why: Paul's commendation of a church for keeping traditions does not illuminate the praise of the capable woman.
1-corinthians-11:2:2.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

1-corinthians-13:4:18.summary: 1 Corinthians 13:4 says “love is patient; love is kind”; Proverbs 31:20 says the woman “opened her hands to a needy person.” Generosity can be seen as kindness, but the texts share no wording and 13:4 does not mention giving or the poor.
1-corinthians-13:4:18.why: The link rests only on a general idea of goodness and adds nothing specific.
1-corinthians-13:4:18.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

1-kings-11:27:9.summary: 1 Kings 11:27 explains how Jeroboam “raised his hands against King Solomon”; Proverbs 30:32 warns that if you “stretch out your hand with fighting, you will be dishonored.”
1-kings-11:27:9.why: The hand-raised-in-conflict wording invites comparison, but Kings does not state the dishonor the proverb predicts.
1-kings-11:27:9.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

1-kings-20:7:5.summary: 1 Kings 20:7 has Jezebel taunt Ahab, “Is this how you now act as king over Israel?”; Proverbs 30:31 ends with “a king addressing a nation.” Only the word “king” is shared.
1-kings-20:7:5.why: Jezebel's scheme over Naboth's vineyard has nothing to do with the stately bearing in the proverb.
1-kings-20:7:5.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

1-kings-6:7:4.summary: 1 Kings 6:7 describes the temple “built of sharply cut, unworked stones” with no iron tool heard; Proverbs 24:27 tells the reader to prepare work and field first and then “you will rebuild your house.” Only the general idea of building a house is shared.
1-kings-6:7:4.why: Proverbs 24:27 is about ordering one's own work, so it adds nothing to the account of the temple's quiet construction.
1-kings-6:7:4.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

1-kings-7:34:1.summary: 1 Kings 7:34 places in the temple “the gold table on which were the loaves of the offering”; Exodus 39:17 lists among the finished tabernacle furnishings “the table of presentation and all its utensils, and the bread of the Presence.”
1-kings-7:34:1.why: Solomon’s temple carries forward the table and its loaves first made for the tabernacle.
1-kings-7:34:1.note: Corrected reading: English Exodus 39:36 (the table and showbread) is Exodus 39:17 in the Saints Greek order; it was previously shown as 39:15 (the altar).

1-kings-7:34:8.summary: 1 Kings 7:34 begins its list with “the gold altar”; Exodus 39:15 lists “the altar and all its utensils, the anointing oil, and the compounded incense” among the furnishings brought to Moses. The Greek list has one altar entry and names it together with the incense.
1-kings-7:34:8.why: It sets the temple’s incense altar beside the tabernacle altar it replaces.
1-kings-7:34:8.note: Corrected reading: English Exodus 39:38 (the golden altar, anointing oil and incense) is Exodus 39:15 in the Saints Greek order; it was previously shown as 39:17 (the table).

1-peter-3:5:7.summary: 1 Peter 3:5 says the holy women “who hoped in God” adorned themselves in that way; Proverbs 31:30 says “beauty is vain” and the understanding woman should “praise the fear of the Lord.” Both locate a woman’s true adornment in devotion to God rather than appearance.
1-peter-3:5:7.why: The proverb gives Old Testament grounding for Peter’s appeal to the example of holy women.
1-peter-3:5:7.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

1-peter-3:5:14.summary: 1 Peter 3:5 commends “the holy women of former times, who hoped in God” and submitted to their husbands; Proverbs 31:10 asks, “A courageous woman—who will find her?” Both praise a woman of worth, but share no specific wording.
1-peter-3:5:14.why: The link reflects a general theme of admirable women rather than a specific connection.
1-peter-3:5:14.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

1-samuel-15:13:10.summary: 1 Samuel 15:13 has Saul greet Samuel, “Blessed are you by the Lord!”; Proverbs 31:31 says, “Give her from the fruits of her hands.” The verses share no wording or subject.
1-samuel-15:13:10.why: Saul's greeting does not illuminate the proverb's call to reward the capable woman.
1-samuel-15:13:10.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

1-samuel-16:7:6.summary: 1 Samuel 16:7 says “do not look at his appearance” because “God looks at the heart”; Proverbs 31:30 says “beauty is vain” and blesses “an understanding woman.” Both refuse to make outward appearance the measure of worth.
1-samuel-16:7:6.why: Together they state the same principle in narrative and in proverb.
1-samuel-16:7:6.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

1-samuel-25:3:1.summary: 1 Samuel 25:3 describes Abigail as having “good understanding” and being very beautiful; Proverbs 31:10 asks, “A courageous woman—who will find her?” Abigail can be read as an example of such a woman, but the verse's terms differ.
1-samuel-25:3:1.why: Abigail offers a possible narrative illustration, though the texts share no wording.
1-samuel-25:3:1.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

1-samuel-25:3:4.summary: 1 Samuel 25:3 says Abigail “had good understanding and was very beautiful”; Proverbs 31:30 says “beauty is vain; for an understanding woman is blessed.”
1-samuel-25:3:4.why: The proverb’s values, understanding over beauty, match what the narrative highlights first in Abigail.
1-samuel-25:3:4.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

1-samuel-25:19:2.summary: 1 Samuel 25:19 says Abigail sent her young men ahead but “did not tell her husband”; Proverbs 31:11–12 says “her husband’s heart is confident in her” and she “works good things for her husband.” Abigail acts for her household’s good, but acting without her husband’s knowledge fits awkwardly with the proverb’s picture of a husband’s confidence.
1-samuel-25:19:2.why: It raises a useful comparison about a wife acting for her household, but the texts do not clearly match.
1-samuel-25:19:2.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

1-samuel-25:39:16.summary: 1 Samuel 25:39 has David send “to take her as his wife” after Abigail's intervention; Proverbs 31:10 asks, “A courageous woman—who will find her?” The link depends on reading Abigail as the rare woman found.
1-samuel-25:39:16.why: The connection is a loose narrative illustration rather than a textual tie.
1-samuel-25:39:16.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

1-samuel-25:39:17.summary: 1 Samuel 25:39 has David say “Blessed be the Lord” and send to take Abigail as his wife; Proverbs 31:30 says “an understanding woman is blessed.” The verse does not mention Abigail’s understanding, so the link depends on the wider chapter rather than the text given.
1-samuel-25:39:17.why: Abigail may be read as an example of the proverb’s ideal, but this verse alone does not show it.
1-samuel-25:39:17.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

1-timothy-1:9:23.summary: 1 Timothy 1:9 lists “those who strike fathers and those who strike mothers” among the lawless; Proverbs 30:17 curses “an eye mocking a father and dishonoring a mother’s old age.” Both condemn abuse of father and mother, though striking and mocking differ and 1 Timothy only names it in a list.
1-timothy-1:9:23.why: The link shows that wrong toward parents is treated as serious in both Testaments, without a closer verbal tie.
1-timothy-1:9:23.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

1-timothy-2:9:13.summary: 1 Timothy 2:9 asks women not to adorn themselves with “costly clothing”; Proverbs 31:22 says the woman made “garments of fine linen and purple for herself.” Both concern women’s clothing, but they point in different directions and neither comments on the other.
1-timothy-2:9:13.why: The pairing raises a question about dress rather than showing a shared teaching.
1-timothy-2:9:13.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

1-timothy-2:10:4.summary: 1 Timothy 2:10 commends “good works, as is fitting for women who profess reverence for God”; Proverbs 31:31 says, “Give her from the fruits of her hands.” Both value a woman's works, but share no specific wording.
1-timothy-2:10:4.why: The link reflects a general esteem for women's good works.
1-timothy-2:10:4.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

1-timothy-5:4:8.summary: 1 Timothy 5:4 tells children and grandchildren to practice godliness at home and “repay their forebears”; Proverbs 31:28 says “her mercy raised up her children.” Hebrew-based Bibles have the children rise and bless their mother, but in the Saints wording only her husband praises her, so the theme of children honoring a parent is not present.
1-timothy-5:4:8.why: Both concern a mother and her children, but the Greek wording removes the closest point of contact.
1-timothy-5:4:8.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

2-chronicles-18:11:0.summary: In 2 Chronicles 18:11 all the prophets assure the king “you will prosper”; Proverbs 24:24–25 condemns whoever says of the impious “He is righteous” and blesses “those who reprove.” The link depends on treating the prophets’ assurance as flattery of a wrongdoer, which the verse itself does not state.
2-chronicles-18:11:0.why: It offers a general proverb about flattering versus reproving that a reader may apply to court prophecy, but the texts share no wording.
2-chronicles-18:11:0.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

2-kings-4:9:1.summary: 2 Kings 4:9 has the Shunammite woman tell her husband, “I know that this is a holy man of God”; Proverbs 31:10–11 praises a courageous woman whose “husband’s heart is confident in her.” Her discernment can illustrate such a wife, but the texts share no wording.
2-kings-4:9:1.why: The link is a loose narrative illustration.
2-kings-4:9:1.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

2-kings-5:25:3.summary: In 2 Kings 5:25 Gehazi answers, “Your slave has not gone here or there”; Proverbs 30:20 describes one who “says she has done nothing improper.” Both show a denial after wrongdoing.
2-kings-5:25:3.why: The proverb names the pattern of Gehazi’s lie, though the subjects (greed and adultery) differ.
2-kings-5:25:3.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

2-kings-6:1:4.summary: The prophets complain that “the place where we dwell … is too narrow for us”; Joshua 19:47a says the Amorites “pressed away from them the boundary of their allotted portion,” leaving Dan without room.
2-kings-6:1:4.why: Both describe a group short of space, but the settings, people and outcomes are unrelated.
2-kings-6:1:4.note: Corrected reading: English Joshua 19:47 corresponds to Joshua 19:47a–48 in the Saints Greek; Joshua 19:47 there is the inheritance summary (English 19:48).

2-peter-1:3:31.summary: 2 Peter 1:3 speaks of God's “glory and excellence”; Proverbs 31:29 says “many did mighty things, but you stand above and have surpassed them all.” The verses share no wording or subject.
2-peter-1:3:31.why: The link depends on English “virtuously” in Proverbs 31:29, which the Saints wording does not use.
2-peter-1:3:31.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

2-peter-1:3:32.summary: 2 Peter 1:3 speaks of God's “own glory and excellence”; Proverbs 31:10 asks, “A courageous woman—who will find her?” The link depends on English renderings such as “virtuous” or “excellent” wife, which the Greek-based “courageous” does not carry.
2-peter-1:3:32.why: In the Saints wording the verses share neither vocabulary nor subject.
2-peter-1:3:32.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

2-samuel-1:23:3.summary: 2 Samuel 1:23 says Saul and Jonathan “proved stronger than lions”; Proverbs 30:30 describes “a lion’s cub, stronger than beasts.” Both use the lion as an image of strength, but in unrelated settings.
2-samuel-1:23:3.why: The shared lion comparison is a common biblical image rather than a specific link.
2-samuel-1:23:3.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

2-samuel-11:2:6.summary: 2 Samuel 11:2 says David saw a woman bathing who “was very beautiful in appearance”; Proverbs 31:30 says “beauty is vain” and blesses “an understanding woman.” The narrative turns on attraction to beauty, which the proverb refuses to treat as decisive.
2-samuel-11:2:6.why: The proverb offers a counterweight to the attraction that drives David’s actions in this scene.
2-samuel-11:2:6.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

2-samuel-11:2:14.summary: 2 Samuel 11:2 says David “rose from his bed” toward evening and saw a woman bathing; Proverbs 24:33–34 warns that “a little I sleep” ends in poverty. The verse does not call David idle or speak of want, so the only link is a reference to rest.
2-samuel-11:2:14.why: Applying the sluggard warning to David here reads a judgment into the narrative that neither text states.
2-samuel-11:2:14.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

2-samuel-11:4:4.summary: 2 Samuel 11:4 notes that the woman David took “was purifying herself from her impurity”; Proverbs 30:20 says an adulterous woman “washes herself and says she has done nothing improper.” Both involve washing in a sexual setting, but Samuel attributes no denial to her.
2-samuel-11:4:4.why: The overlap is a detail of washing; reading the proverb’s self-justification into the Samuel account would go beyond the text.
2-samuel-11:4:4.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

2-samuel-13:1:13.summary: 2 Samuel 13:1 introduces Tamar as “very beautiful in appearance” and says Amnon “loved her”; Proverbs 31:30 says “beauty is vain” and praises understanding and the fear of the Lord. The narrative’s desire rests on appearance, which the proverb calls vain.
2-samuel-13:1:13.why: The proverb exposes the shallow basis of the attraction that begins this narrative.
2-samuel-13:1:13.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

2-samuel-14:22:7.summary: 2 Samuel 14:22 has Joab bow and bless the king for granting his request; Proverbs 31:28 says the woman’s mercy raised up her children and “her husband praised her.” Beyond an act of praise, the passages share no subject or wording.
2-samuel-14:22:7.why: A courtier thanking a king does not illuminate a husband’s praise of his wife.
2-samuel-14:22:7.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

2-samuel-14:25:6.summary: 2 Samuel 14:25 says no man was “so highly praised as Absalom,” without blemish from head to foot; Proverbs 31:30 says “beauty is vain” and calls for praise of “the fear of the Lord.” The contrast of praise for appearance with praise for reverence is apt, but the proverb speaks of a woman and the verse of a man’s public fame.
2-samuel-14:25:6.why: It invites a reader to question praise based on looks, though the two texts are not closely tied.
2-samuel-14:25:6.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

2-samuel-15:3:13.summary: 2 Samuel 15:3 records Absalom telling petitioners “no one from the king is here to hear you”; Proverbs 30:17 curses “an eye mocking a father.” The verse itself says nothing of a father or of mockery.
2-samuel-15:3:13.why: Without wording about parents, the verse does not illustrate the proverb; any link depends on the wider story of Absalom's revolt.
2-samuel-15:3:13.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

2-samuel-18:9:1.summary: 2 Samuel 18:9 tells how Absalom's head caught in the oak and “he hung between heaven and earth”; Proverbs 30:17 says a father-mocking eye will be pecked out by “ravens from the ravines.” The connection rests on Absalom's rebellion against his father, which this verse does not mention, and the punishments differ.
2-samuel-18:9:1.why: It offers a broad example of a rebellious son's ruin, not a specific fulfilment of the proverb.
2-samuel-18:9:1.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

2-samuel-24:6:2.summary: The census route reaches “Danidan and Oudan”; Joshua 19:47a–48 describes Dan hemmed in by the Amorites and a capture of “Lachish,” renamed “Lasendak.” Neither verse names the northern city of Dan.
2-samuel-24:6:2.why: In English Bibles the link is the city of Dan named in Joshua 19:47, but this edition’s wording does not contain that name, so the passages cannot be compared on it.
2-samuel-24:6:2.note: Corrected reading: English Joshua 19:47 corresponds to Joshua 19:47a–48 in the Saints Greek; Joshua 19:47 there is the inheritance summary (English 19:48).

2-samuel-4:5:0.summary: 2 Samuel 4:5 tells of Mephibosheth “sleeping in bed at midday” when his attackers entered; Proverbs 24:33–34 warns that dozing lets poverty arrive “like a good runner.” Both show harm overtaking a sleeper, but the narrative does not present the midday rest as laziness or speak of poverty.
2-samuel-4:5:0.why: It offers a loose illustration of danger arriving while one sleeps, not a shared teaching.
2-samuel-4:5:0.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

2-thessalonians-3:10:5.summary: 2 Thessalonians 3:10 rules that anyone “not willing to work” should “not eat”; Proverbs 24:33–34 warns that “a little I doze, a little I sleep” ends with “your poverty will come marching in front.” Both tie refusal of work directly to lack of provision.
2-thessalonians-3:10:5.why: The proverb supplies the older wisdom behind Paul’s command that idleness should bear its own consequence.
2-thessalonians-3:10:5.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

acts-9:39:1.summary: In Acts 9:39 the widows show “the tunics and garments Dorcas had made”; Proverbs 31:31 says, “Give her from the fruits of her hands.”
acts-9:39:1.why: The widows’ display of Dorcas’s work enacts the proverb’s call to honor a woman by the work of her hands.
acts-9:39:1.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

colossians-3:20:7.summary: Colossians 3:20 says “Children, obey your parents in all things”; Proverbs 30:17 curses “an eye mocking a father and dishonoring a mother’s old age.” Both concern a child's duty to parents, one stated positively and one by its violation.
colossians-3:20:7.why: The pairing reflects the general duty toward parents but shares no distinctive wording.
colossians-3:20:7.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

daniel-11:20:3.summary: Daniel 11:20 foretells a ruler “shattered, but not in wrath or war”; Proverbs 30:33 says that if you “drag out words, disputes and battles will come out.” The only contact is the general idea of war.
daniel-11:20:3.why: A prophecy about a king’s downfall and a proverb about provoking quarrels do not inform each other.
daniel-11:20:3.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

deuteronomy-1:17:3.summary: Deuteronomy 1:17 commands, “You shall not show partiality in judgment” and not to “shrink before the face of man”; Proverbs 24:23 says “to show deference to a face in judgment is not good.”
deuteronomy-1:17:3.why: Both use the language of a person’s “face” in judgment to forbid partiality, so the proverb echoes Moses’ charge to Israel’s judges.
deuteronomy-1:17:3.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

deuteronomy-16:19:6.summary: Deuteronomy 16:19 forbids judges to “show partiality” or “pervert judgment”; Proverbs 24:23 teaches that “to show deference to a face in judgment is not good.”
deuteronomy-16:19:6.why: Both name the same specific fault, favoring persons when rendering judgment, so the proverb restates the law’s standard for judges.
deuteronomy-16:19:6.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

deuteronomy-16:19:23.summary: Deuteronomy 16:19 forbids judges to “pervert judgment” or take bribes; Proverbs 24:28 says “Do not be a false witness against your fellow citizen.” Both protect justice in disputes, but one addresses judges and bribery, the other a witness's testimony.
deuteronomy-16:19:23.why: The link shows a common concern for honest legal proceedings without sharing a specific teaching.
deuteronomy-16:19:23.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

deuteronomy-21:11:0.summary: Deuteronomy 21:11 describes a man who sees “a woman fair of countenance” and would “take her unto yourself for a wife”; Proverbs 31:30 says a woman’s “beauty is vain” and that “an understanding woman is blessed.” The law addresses choosing a wife for her looks; the proverb names a better basis.
deuteronomy-21:11:0.why: The proverb sets wisdom and reverence against appearance as grounds for choosing a wife.
deuteronomy-21:11:0.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

deuteronomy-21:11:2.summary: Deuteronomy 21:11 regulates taking a captive “woman fair of countenance” as a wife; Proverbs 31:10 asks, “A courageous woman—who will find her?” Outward beauty and courage are different qualities.
deuteronomy-21:11:2.why: The law about captive women does not illuminate the proverb's praise of a rare woman.
deuteronomy-21:11:2.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

deuteronomy-21:18:10.summary: Deuteronomy 21:18 describes a “disobedient and rebellious son” who does not hearken to “the voice of his father or the voice of his mother”; Proverbs 30:17 curses “an eye mocking a father and dishonoring a mother.” Both treat a son's contempt for both parents as a grave offence.
deuteronomy-21:18:10.why: The Law's case of the rebellious son gives the legal background to the proverb's curse.
deuteronomy-21:18:10.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

deuteronomy-33:22:0.summary: Moses calls Dan “a lion’s cub” that “shall leap forth from Bashan”; Joshua 19:47a instead shows Dan unable to drive out the Amorites, who “did not allow them to descend into the valley.”
deuteronomy-33:22:0.why: Read together they contrast the blessing’s vigour with Dan’s actual struggle for land, but the connection is only the tribe itself.
deuteronomy-33:22:0.note: Corrected reading: English Joshua 19:47 corresponds to Joshua 19:47a–48 in the Saints Greek; Joshua 19:47 there is the inheritance summary (English 19:48).

deuteronomy-34:1:4.summary: The Lord shows Moses the land “of Gilead unto Dan”; Joshua 19:47a–48 tells of Dan pressed by the Amorites and of a city called “Lasendak.” The place-name Dan does not appear in the Joshua reading.
deuteronomy-34:1:4.why: The English link depends on Joshua 19:47 renaming a city Dan; this edition’s reading has no such renaming.
deuteronomy-34:1:4.note: Corrected reading: English Joshua 19:47 corresponds to Joshua 19:47a–48 in the Saints Greek; Joshua 19:47 there is the inheritance summary (English 19:48).

ecclesiastes-1:8:9.summary: Ecclesiastes 1:8 says “the eye will not be filled with seeing, nor the ear filled with hearing”; Proverbs 30:15–16 lists things that are not filled and never say “It is enough.” Both use the language of never being filled, but Ecclesiastes speaks of the weariness of human experience and Proverbs of insatiable appetites.
ecclesiastes-1:8:9.why: The shared motif of never being filled is real but serves different points.
ecclesiastes-1:8:9.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

ecclesiastes-10:7:2.summary: Ecclesiastes 10:7 reports “slaves on horses and rulers walking like slaves”; Proverbs 30:22 lists “a household servant becomes king” among things the earth cannot bear. Both treat a servant raised to rule as an inversion of proper order.
ecclesiastes-10:7:2.why: Each text helps interpret the other’s picture of social order turned upside down.
ecclesiastes-10:7:2.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

ecclesiastes-10:18:1.summary: Ecclesiastes 10:18 says that “through laziness the roof beams will sink” and the house “will leak”; Proverbs 24:31 pictures a field left alone that becomes “wasteland” with “stone fences … torn down,” and 24:33–34 links dozing to poverty. Both use the decay of neglected property to show what idleness produces.
ecclesiastes-10:18:1.why: The two images of a leaking house and a ruined field reinforce each other as pictures of slow loss through neglect.
ecclesiastes-10:18:1.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

ecclesiastes-4:5:7.summary: Ecclesiastes 4:5 says “the fool folded his hands and ate his own flesh”; Proverbs 24:33 has the idler “clasp my chest with my hands,” and 24:34 brings poverty. Both use the gesture of idle, folded hands to show a fool consuming himself through inaction.
ecclesiastes-4:5:7.why: The shared gesture lets each saying illustrate the self-destruction described in the other.
ecclesiastes-4:5:7.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

ecclesiastes-5:9:12.summary: Ecclesiastes 5:9 says “whoever loves silver will not be filled with silver”; Proverbs 30:15–16 names things, including “a woman’s desire,” that “did not fill her” and never say “It is enough.” Both describe desire that is never satisfied by what it gets.
ecclesiastes-5:9:12.why: The proverb’s list widens Ecclesiastes’ point about greed into a picture of appetite that cannot be filled.
ecclesiastes-5:9:12.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

ecclesiastes-6:9:11.summary: Ecclesiastes 6:9 prefers “a sight for the eyes” over “wandering in appetite”; Proverbs 30:15–16 lists insatiable things that never say “Enough!” Both touch on restless appetite, but the texts share no distinctive wording.
ecclesiastes-6:9:11.why: It points to a general theme of unsatisfied desire rather than a specific link.
ecclesiastes-6:9:11.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

ecclesiastes-8:3:9.summary: Ecclesiastes 8:3 warns that the ruler “will do whatever he pleases”; Proverbs 30:31 lists “a king addressing a nation” among things of stately bearing. The Hebrew of Proverbs 30:31 describes a king no one can resist, but the Saints reading lacks that idea.
ecclesiastes-8:3:9.why: In the Greek wording the proverb does not speak of irresistible royal power, so the link does not hold.
ecclesiastes-8:3:9.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

ecclesiastes-8:4:12.summary: Ecclesiastes 8:4 says “a king with authority speaks; and who will say to him, ‘What will you do?’”; Proverbs 30:31 ends with “a king addressing a nation.” Both picture a king speaking with authority, but the Greek proverb lacks the Hebrew idea that no one can rise against him.
ecclesiastes-8:4:12.why: The link is limited to the image of a king speaking.
ecclesiastes-8:4:12.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

ephesians-6:1:12.summary: Ephesians 6:1 says “Children, obey your parents in the Lord”; Proverbs 30:17 curses “an eye mocking a father and dishonoring a mother’s old age.” Both concern conduct toward parents, from opposite sides.
ephesians-6:1:12.why: The link shows only the general duty toward parents, without shared wording.
ephesians-6:1:12.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

esther-1:11:0.summary: Esther 1:11 has the king summon the queen “to show all the rulers and the nations her beauty”; Proverbs 31:30 says “beauty is vain” and praises the woman of understanding. The king values the queen for display of her looks, which the proverb discounts.
esther-1:11:0.why: The proverb highlights how the king’s treatment of the queen rests on a value it calls vain.
esther-1:11:0.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

esther-7:6:14.summary: Esther 7:6 has Esther openly name “this wicked Haman” before the king; Proverbs 24:24–25 curses calling the impious “righteous” and promises that “those who reprove will appear better.” Esther’s accusation is an example of reproof, but the connection is a general principle rather than shared wording.
esther-7:6:14.why: The proverb gives a moral frame for Esther’s courage in naming the wicked, though it is only loosely tied to the scene.
esther-7:6:14.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

exodus-10:4:8.summary: Exodus 10:4 threatens “many locusts upon all your borders”; Proverbs 30:27 observes that “the locust is without a king, yet marches out in good order.” Both mention locusts, but Exodus announces a plague while Proverbs draws a lesson from their orderly movement.
exodus-10:4:8.why: The shared creature is a real point of contact, but the passages use it for different purposes.
exodus-10:4:8.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

exodus-20:12:6.summary: Exodus 20:12 commands, “Honour your father and your mother”; Proverbs 30:17 curses the eye “mocking a father and dishonoring a mother’s old age.” The proverb describes the very dishonor the commandment forbids.
exodus-20:12:6.why: Proverbs 30:17 shows the consequence of breaking the fifth commandment.
exodus-20:12:6.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

exodus-21:15:0.summary: Exodus 21:15 rules that “He who strikes his father or his mother shall surely be put to death”; Proverbs 30:17 says the eye mocking a father and dishonoring a mother will be devoured by ravens and eagles. Both attach severe punishment to wrongs against both parents.
exodus-21:15:0.why: The Law's death penalty and the proverb's curse together show how seriously contempt for parents is judged.
exodus-21:15:0.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

exodus-21:16:6.summary: Exodus 21:16 says “He who reviles his father or his mother shall surely die”; Proverbs 30:17 curses “an eye mocking a father and dishonoring a mother’s old age.” Both address contempt toward parents and pronounce death on it.
exodus-21:16:6.why: Proverbs 30:17 restates the Law's verdict on reviling parents in vivid poetic form.
exodus-21:16:6.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

exodus-23:1:33.summary: Exodus 23:1 commands, “You shall not … become an unrighteous witness”; Proverbs 24:28 says, “Do not be a false witness against your fellow citizen.” Both prohibit giving dishonest testimony.
exodus-23:1:33.why: Proverbs 24:28 restates the Law's ban on false witness as personal wisdom toward one's neighbor.
exodus-23:1:33.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

exodus-25:30:2.summary: Exodus 25:30 commands “the bread of the Presence on the table”; Exodus 39:17 reports “the table of presentation and all its utensils, and the bread of the Presence” among the completed work.
exodus-25:30:2.why: It shows the instruction for the table and its bread carried out in the finished tabernacle.
exodus-25:30:2.note: Corrected reading: English Exodus 39:36 (the table and showbread) is Exodus 39:17 in the Saints Greek order; it was previously shown as 39:15 (the altar).

exodus-26:14:8.summary: Exodus 26:14 commands “a covering … of rams’ skins dyed red, with coverings of blue skins”; Exodus 39:20 lists “the leather coverings of rams’ skins dyed red, the coverings of blue skins” among the finished work brought to Moses.
exodus-26:14:8.why: It confirms that the covering commanded for the tabernacle was made as specified.
exodus-26:14:8.note: Corrected reading: English Exodus 39:34 (the coverings) is Exodus 39:20 in the Saints Greek order; it was previously reported as unavailable.

exodus-28:17:12.summary: Exodus 28:17 describes rows of stones, “a sardius, topaz, and emerald,” on the priestly garment; Proverbs 31:10 says such a woman is “more precious than costly stones.” The stones in Exodus are not used as a measure of value.
exodus-28:17:12.why: A shared mention of gemstones does not connect the priestly vestment to the proverb.
exodus-28:17:12.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

exodus-28:40:0.summary: Exodus 28:40 commands tunics, sashes and turbans “for Aaron’s sons”; Exodus 39:18 lists “Aaron’s robes for the sanctuary and his sons’ robes for priestly service” among the finished work.
exodus-28:40:0.why: It shows the garments commanded for the priests completed and presented to Moses.
exodus-28:40:0.note: Corrected reading: English Exodus 39:41 (the priestly garments) is Exodus 39:18 in the Saints Greek order; it was previously shown as 39:21 (the pegs).

exodus-35:19:1.summary: Exodus 35:19 lists “the holy robes of Aaron the priest … the priestly tunics for Aaron’s sons” among the work to be done; Exodus 39:18 records “Aaron’s robes for the sanctuary and his sons’ robes for priestly service” as completed.
exodus-35:19:1.why: The commissioning list and the completion list name the same garments, showing the work finished as ordered.
exodus-35:19:1.note: Corrected reading: English Exodus 39:41 (the priestly garments) is Exodus 39:18 in the Saints Greek order; it was previously shown as 39:21 (the pegs).

exodus-35:25:10.summary: Exodus 35:25 says “Every woman wise in heart spun with her hands” and brought “purple” and “fine linen”; Proverbs 31:19 says she “braces her hands on a spindle,” and 31:22 mentions “fine linen and purple.”
exodus-35:25:10.why: Both honor women’s skilled spinning and cloth-making, sharing the same materials and handwork.
exodus-35:25:10.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

exodus-36:8:9.summary: Exodus 36:8 says the craftsmen “made the holy robes for Aaron the priest”; Exodus 39:18 lists “Aaron’s robes for the sanctuary” among the work brought to Moses.
exodus-36:8:9.why: It follows the robes from their making to their presentation.
exodus-36:8:9.note: Corrected reading: English Exodus 39:41 (the priestly garments) is Exodus 39:18 in the Saints Greek order; it was previously shown as 39:21 (the pegs).

exodus-40:9:12.summary: Exodus 40:9 commands Moses to “take the anointing oil” and sanctify the tent “and all its utensils”; Exodus 39:15 lists “the altar and all its utensils, the anointing oil” among the finished items.
exodus-40:9:12.why: The oil and the utensils presented as complete are the ones Moses is told to use in consecrating the tent.
exodus-40:9:12.note: Corrected reading: English Exodus 39:39 (the bronze altar) corresponds to the single altar entry, Exodus 39:15, in the Saints Greek order; it was previously shown as 39:18 (Aaron’s robes).

ezekiel-16:10:20.summary: Ezekiel 16:10 describes the Lord clothing Jerusalem with “blue-purple footwear” and “fine linen”; Proverbs 31:22 says the woman made “garments of fine linen and purple.” The fine textiles match, but the actions and settings differ.
ezekiel-16:10:20.why: Shared fabrics show what fine clothing looked like but do not establish a common teaching.
ezekiel-16:10:20.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

ezekiel-18:16:1.summary: Ezekiel 18:16 describes the righteous man who “gave his bread to the hungry and clothed the naked”; Proverbs 31:20 says the woman “opened her hands to a needy person and stretched out her wrist to a poor person.” Both name practical giving to the needy as a mark of righteousness.
ezekiel-18:16:1.why: Together they show concrete generosity as part of the righteous life for both man and woman.
ezekiel-18:16:1.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

ezekiel-22:7:12.summary: Ezekiel 22:7 charges Jerusalem, “They reviled father and mother in you”; Proverbs 30:17 curses “an eye mocking a father and dishonoring a mother.” Both name contempt for father and mother as a serious sin.
ezekiel-22:7:12.why: Ezekiel counts among Jerusalem's sins the offence Proverbs 30:17 curses.
ezekiel-22:7:12.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

genesis-16:4:0.summary: Genesis 16:4 says that when Hagar conceived, “her mistress was dishonoured in her sight”; Proverbs 30:23 lists among unbearable things “if a maidservant casts out her own mistress.” Hagar's contempt for Sarai fits the proverb's maidservant who sets herself over her mistress, though Hagar does not cast Sarai out.
genesis-16:4:0.why: The story gives a concrete instance of the household upheaval the proverb describes.
genesis-16:4:0.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

genesis-16:4:5.summary: Genesis 16:4 tells how Hagar conceived and her mistress “was dishonoured in her sight”; Proverbs 30:20–21 describes an adulterous woman’s denial and introduces things by which “the earth is shaken.” The verses given do not mention a servant or a mistress.
genesis-16:4:5.why: Any link would depend on a later verse of the numerical saying, which is outside this range, so the reference as given does not help.
genesis-16:4:5.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

genesis-2:24:8.summary: Genesis 2:24 says a man shall “cleave to his wife”; Proverbs 31:10 asks, “A courageous woman—who will find her?” Proverbs 31:10 does not speak of marriage itself.
genesis-2:24:8.why: The institution of marriage is too general a theme to connect the two verses.
genesis-2:24:8.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

genesis-27:43:5.summary: Genesis 27:43 has Rebekah tell Jacob, “my child, obey my voice,” and flee to Laban; Proverbs 30:17 curses an eye “mocking a father and dishonoring a mother.” Rebekah's urgent instruction concerns escape from Esau, not honor toward parents.
genesis-27:43:5.why: The incidental mention of obeying a mother does not illuminate the proverb's curse.
genesis-27:43:5.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

genesis-28:7:1.summary: Genesis 28:7 notes that “Jacob had obeyed his father and his mother”; Proverbs 30:17 curses “an eye mocking a father and dishonoring a mother.” Jacob's obedience is the opposite of the conduct the proverb condemns.
genesis-28:7:1.why: It gives a narrative example of honoring parents, but the contrast is general.
genesis-28:7:1.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

genesis-29:17:8.summary: Genesis 29:17 notes that “Leah’s eyes were weak, but Rachel was beautiful in form”; Proverbs 31:30 says “beauty is vain.” The verse only describes the sisters’ appearance and makes no judgment that the proverb answers.
genesis-29:17:8.why: The proverb can be brought to the story, but the verse itself gives only a description of beauty.
genesis-29:17:8.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

genesis-30:13:1.summary: Genesis 30:13 has Leah say “women shall call me blessed”; Proverbs 31:28 says “her husband praised her.” Hebrew-based Bibles have the children call the woman blessed, but the Saints wording does not use that phrase, leaving only the general idea of a woman being praised.
genesis-30:13:1.why: The Greek wording removes the shared phrase, so the link is loose.
genesis-30:13:1.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

genesis-33:9:10.summary: In Genesis 33:9 Esau says, “I have much, brother; let what is yours be yours”; Proverbs 30:15 describes a leech whose daughters were never filled and “not content to say, ‘Enough!’” The Saints text of Genesis has “I have much,” not the word “enough” found in Hebrew-based translations.
genesis-33:9:10.why: Esau’s willingness to decline more stands loosely against the proverb’s picture of insatiable appetite.
genesis-33:9:10.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

genesis-34:13:1.summary: Genesis 34:13 says Jacob's sons answered Shechem and Hamor “with deceit” because Dinah had been defiled; Proverbs 24:29 forbids saying, “As he treated me, I will treat him, and I will punish him for the wrong he did me,” after 24:28 warns against falsehood toward a fellow citizen. The sons' deceitful revenge is the conduct the proverb rejects.
genesis-34:13:1.why: The narrative gives a concrete case of the deceit and retaliation that Proverbs 24:28–29 warns against.
genesis-34:13:1.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

genesis-34:20:9.summary: Genesis 34:20 has Hamor and Shechem come “to the gate of their city” to speak to the men; Proverbs 31:23 says her husband “becomes distinguished in the gates when he sits in council.” Both show the city gate as the place of public deliberation.
genesis-34:20:9.why: The link illustrates the gate's civic role but has no further connection.
genesis-34:20:9.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

genesis-37:25:13.summary: Genesis 37:25 describes Joseph’s brothers sitting “to eat bread” as Ishmaelite traders approach; Proverbs 30:20 describes “the way of an adulterous woman.” The texts share no wording or subject.
genesis-37:25:13.why: Nothing in the caravan scene relates to the proverb’s picture of denial after adultery.
genesis-37:25:13.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

genesis-39:6:3.summary: Genesis 39:6 says Potiphar “committed all that he had into Joseph’s hands” and concerned himself with nothing else; Proverbs 31:11 says “Her husband’s heart is confident in her.” Both show a household entrusted to a reliable manager.
genesis-39:6:3.why: The theme of trusted household oversight is shared, but the persons and relationships are quite different.
genesis-39:6:3.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

genesis-40:19:11.summary: Genesis 40:19 foretells that “the birds of heaven shall eat your flesh”; Proverbs 30:17 says “ravens from the ravines” will peck out the mocking eye and “young eagles devour it.” Both use birds devouring a body as a picture of punishment, but Genesis has no concern with parents.
genesis-40:19:11.why: The shared image of carrion birds as judgment is the only point of contact.
genesis-40:19:11.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

genesis-41:42:8.summary: Genesis 41:42 says Pharaoh clothed Joseph “in a robe of fine linen”; Proverbs 31:22 says the woman made “garments of fine linen and purple for herself.” Fine linen is the only shared element between a royal investiture and a household’s clothing.
genesis-41:42:8.why: The common fabric is incidental and does not clarify either passage.
genesis-41:42:8.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

genesis-43:2:0.summary: Genesis 43:2 has Jacob tell his sons to “buy us a little food”; Proverbs 31:16 says the woman inspected a farm and “bought it.” The word buy is the only link between a famine errand and a land purchase.
genesis-43:2:0.why: The shared verb does not connect the two situations.
genesis-43:2:0.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

genesis-48:12:3.summary: Genesis 48:12 says Joseph’s sons were brought from his knees and “bowed down before him”; Proverbs 31:28 says the woman’s mercy “raised up her children” and her husband praised her. The texts share no meaningful wording or subject.
genesis-48:12:3.why: Grandsons bowing before Jacob does not connect with a mother’s care for her children.
genesis-48:12:3.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

genesis-9:20:10.summary: Genesis 9:20 reports that Noah “planted a vineyard”; Proverbs 24:30 compares “a person lacking understanding” to “a vineyard.” The only common element is the word vineyard, used for a literal planting in one and a simile for folly in the other.
genesis-9:20:10.why: The shared word does not bear on either passage’s meaning, so the link does not help a reader.
genesis-9:20:10.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

genesis-9:22:0.summary: Genesis 9:22 says Ham “saw his father’s nakedness, and went out and told his two brothers”; Proverbs 30:17 curses “an eye mocking a father.” Ham's looking and telling is a narrative case of a son's eye dishonoring his father.
genesis-9:22:0.why: The story of Ham supplies a concrete example of the contempt the proverb condemns.
genesis-9:22:0.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

hebrews-12:9:11.summary: Hebrews 12:9 recalls that “we had our fathers in the flesh to discipline us, and we respected them”; Proverbs 30:17 curses an eye “mocking a father.” Respect for fathers is common ground, but Hebrews uses it to argue for submission to God.
hebrews-12:9:11.why: The link is a general contrast between respect and mockery of fathers.
hebrews-12:9:11.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

hebrews-6:12:7.summary: Hebrews 6:12 urges readers not to “become sluggish” but to imitate those who “inherit the promises”; Proverbs 24:33–34 warns that dozing brings poverty. Both oppose sluggishness, but Hebrews concerns perseverance in faith while Proverbs concerns material neglect.
hebrews-6:12:7.why: It gives a practical picture of sluggishness, though the spiritual inheritance in Hebrews is a different subject.
hebrews-6:12:7.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

hosea-12:9:9.summary: In Hosea 12:9 Ephraim says, “I have become rich; I have found refreshment for myself,” despite “the injustices in which he sinned”; Proverbs 30:20 describes one who “says she has done nothing improper.” The Greek of Hosea has no explicit claim of innocence, leaving only self-satisfaction in the face of sin.
hosea-12:9:9.why: Both show complacency after wrongdoing, but the specific denial that ties them in Hebrew-based translations is missing here.
hosea-12:9:9.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

hosea-4:18:0.summary: Hosea 4:18 in the Saints wording says “He chose Canaanites. They prostituted themselves thoroughly”; Proverbs 30:15–16 lists insatiable things such as the leech and Hades. The Greek of Hosea lacks the wording that links the verses in some Hebrew-based Bibles, and nothing else connects them.
hosea-4:18:0.why: Apart from an incidental use of “loved,” the passages do not share a subject.
hosea-4:18:0.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

isaiah-5:14:0.summary: Isaiah 5:14 says “Hades enlarged its appetite and opened its mouth without ceasing”; Proverbs 30:16 lists “Hades” among things that will never say “It is enough.” Both portray Hades as a mouth that is never satisfied.
isaiah-5:14:0.why: The shared image of insatiable Hades helps a reader see the judgment in Isaiah as death’s unending appetite.
isaiah-5:14:0.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

isaiah-5:23:12.summary: Isaiah 5:23 condemns those “who justify the ungodly for gifts”; Proverbs 24:24 says one who says of the impious, “He is righteous,” will be “accursed among peoples.”
isaiah-5:23:12.why: Both condemn acquitting the wicked; Isaiah names bribery as the motive, while the proverb names the public curse that follows.
isaiah-5:23:12.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

isaiah-56:10:12.summary: Isaiah 56:10 calls the watchmen blind men who “did not know how to think,” “loving to doze”; Proverbs 24:30 speaks of “a person lacking understanding,” and 24:33 of one who says “a little I doze.” Both join lack of understanding with a love of dozing that leads to neglect.
isaiah-56:10:12.why: The proverb’s account of where dozing leads sharpens Isaiah’s charge against negligent watchmen.
isaiah-56:10:12.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

james-2:1:0.summary: James 2:1 forbids holding the faith “with acts of favoritism”; Proverbs 24:23 says “to show deference to a face in judgment is not good.”
james-2:1:0.why: Both reject favoring people by their standing, and the proverb shows James applying an old wisdom standard to the life of the church.
james-2:1:0.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

jeremiah-2:23:10.summary: Jeremiah 2:23 asks, “How will you say, I was not polluted and did not follow Baal?”; Proverbs 30:20 describes an adulterous woman who “says she has done nothing improper.”
jeremiah-2:23:10.why: Both expose a claim of innocence that contradicts conduct, and the proverb fits Jeremiah’s picture of Israel as an unfaithful partner.
jeremiah-2:23:10.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

jeremiah-22:14:6.summary: Jeremiah 22:14 describes a king who “built yourself a well-proportioned house” paneled with cedar; Proverbs 24:27 says to prepare work and field and then “you will rebuild your house.” Both concern building a house, but Jeremiah condemns royal extravagance while Proverbs teaches the right order of work.
jeremiah-22:14:6.why: The shared subject of housebuilding gives a loose contrast between building in proper order and building for show, but no specific teaching connects them.
jeremiah-22:14:6.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

jeremiah-27:8:6.summary: Jeremiah 27:8 tells the exiles to come out of Babylon and “become like dragons before sheep”; Proverbs 30:31 includes “a male goat leading a flock.” In Hebrew both verses use the he-goat leading the flock, but the Greek Jeremiah has “dragons,” leaving only the image of going before the sheep.
jeremiah-27:8:6.why: The Greek wording reduces a shared image to a loose likeness.
jeremiah-27:8:6.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

job-13:8:0.summary: Job 13:8 asks, “Will you shrink back? Become judges yourselves”; Proverbs 24:23 warns against showing “deference to a face in judgment.” The partiality wording found in Hebrew-based translations of Job is not present in the Saints text, leaving only the shared idea of judging.
job-13:8:0.why: The proverb can sharpen Job’s challenge to his friends as judges, but the verse itself does not mention favoritism in this edition.
job-13:8:0.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

job-15:24:0.summary: Job 15:24 says distress will hold the wicked “like a general falling in the front rank”; Proverbs 24:34 says “your poverty will come marching in front.” Both use military imagery for trouble advancing, but the pictures differ and the subjects are not the same.
job-15:24:0.why: The military image is a loose echo; it does not explain either verse.
job-15:24:0.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

job-21:5:3.summary: Job 21:5 says, “Look at me and be amazed, placing a hand upon your cheek”; Proverbs 30:32 warns against stretching out “your hand with fighting.” The Greek of 30:32 has no hand-over-mouth gesture of silence, which is the link in Hebrew-based translations.
job-21:5:3.why: A gesture of astonishment and a hand raised to fight are different actions, so the shared word “hand” does not connect them.
job-21:5:3.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

job-28:18:1.summary: Greek Job 28:18 says “Lofty things and gabis will not be mentioned; draw wisdom beyond the innermost things”; Proverbs 31:10 says such a woman is “more precious than costly stones.” The Hebrew link (both valued above the same gems) is obscured in the Greek, leaving only a comparison of worth.
job-28:18:1.why: Both set something above costly things, but the Greek wording leaves the connection loose.
job-28:18:1.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

job-29:9:3.summary: Job 29:9 recalls powerful men “placing a finger upon their mouths”; Proverbs 30:32 warns against stretching out “your hand with fighting.” The Greek of 30:32 lacks the gesture of silence found in Hebrew-based translations.
job-29:9:3.why: Without that gesture the proverb is about quarrelling, not keeping silent, so it does not illuminate Job’s scene.
job-29:9:3.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

job-32:21:8.summary: In Job 32:21 Elihu will not be “ashamed before a human” or “overawed by a mortal”; Proverbs 24:23 condemns showing “deference to a face in judgment.” Both resist deferring to persons, but Elihu speaks of his own frankness, not of a court.
job-32:21:8.why: The proverb gives a general principle behind Elihu’s refusal to be swayed by people, though the settings differ.
job-32:21:8.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

job-40:4:0.summary: In Job 40:4 Job says, “I will place a hand over my mouth”; Proverbs 30:32 warns that if you “stretch out your hand with fighting, you will be dishonored.” The Greek of 30:32 has no hand-over-mouth instruction, which is the link in Hebrew-based translations.
job-40:4:0.why: Job’s humble silence and the proverb’s warning against fighting are different acts, so the link does not hold in this edition.
job-40:4:0.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

joel-1:6:6.summary: Joel 1:6 describes an invading “nation” that is “strong and uncountable”; Proverbs 30:26 calls the rock badgers “a nation without strength,” and 30:27 says “the locust is without a king, yet marches out in good order.”
joel-1:6:6.why: The shared “nation” and strength language offers a contrast between a fearsome host and small creatures, but the passages make different points.
joel-1:6:6.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

joel-2:7:0.summary: Joel 2:7 describes invaders who run “like fighters,” each on “his own road,” who “will not turn aside from their paths”; Proverbs 30:27 says the locust “marches out in good order at one command.” Both picture a disciplined host advancing in unbroken order.
joel-2:7:0.why: The proverb’s locust image helps a reader see the orderly, unstoppable advance Joel describes.
joel-2:7:0.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

john-2:1:1.summary: John 2:1 records “a wedding … in Cana of Galilee”; Proverbs 31:10–12 praises a courageous woman who “works good things for her husband.” A wedding setting is the only common ground.
john-2:1:1.why: The Cana narrative does not illuminate the portrait of the capable wife.
john-2:1:1.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

john-7:24:4.summary: John 7:24 says, “Do not judge according to appearance, but judge with righteous judgment”; Proverbs 24:23 says “to show deference to a face in judgment is not good.”
john-7:24:4.why: Both warn against judging by outward appearance, so Jesus’ command stands in line with the proverb’s rule for fair judgment.
john-7:24:4.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

joshua-22:21:1.summary: Joshua 22:21 introduces the eastern tribes as they “answered” Israel’s commanders; Proverbs 24:26 says “lips answering good words will kiss.” The verb “answer” is the only common element.
joshua-22:21:1.why: Joshua 22:21 only introduces a speech, so the proverb adds nothing to it without reading in the content of the reply.
joshua-22:21:1.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

jude-1:8:17.summary: Jude 1:8 says false teachers “reject dominion, and slander glorious ones”; Proverbs 30:17 curses an eye “mocking a father and dishonoring a mother.” Jude speaks of contempt for spiritual authorities, not parents.
jude-1:8:17.why: Contempt in general is too broad a theme to connect these verses.
jude-1:8:17.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

judges-1:34:0.summary: Judges 1:34 says “the Amorites pressed the sons of Dan into the mountain, for they did not allow them to come down into the valley”; Joshua 19:47a says the Amorites were “pressing them in the hill country” and “did not allow them to descend into the valley.”
judges-1:34:0.why: The two books give closely matching accounts of why Dan could not hold its allotted land.
judges-1:34:0.note: Corrected reading: English Joshua 19:47 corresponds to Joshua 19:47a–48 in the Saints Greek; Joshua 19:47 there is the inheritance summary (English 19:48).

judges-16:10:3.summary: Judges 16:10 has Delilah complain that Samson “spoken falsehoods to me”; Proverbs 24:28 forbids being “a false witness against your fellow citizen.” Samson's evasion is not testimony against a neighbor.
judges-16:10:3.why: The shared idea of falsehood is too general to illuminate either text.
judges-16:10:3.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

judges-18:7:0.summary: Dan’s scouts find Laish living “in confidence”; Joshua 19:47a explains that the Amorites “pressed away from them the boundary of their allotted portion.” The Joshua reading does not mention Laish.
judges-18:7:0.why: Dan’s lost territory is the background for its search for new land, but the passages share no specific event.
judges-18:7:0.note: Corrected reading: English Joshua 19:47 corresponds to Joshua 19:47a–48 in the Saints Greek; Joshua 19:47 there is the inheritance summary (English 19:48).

judges-18:19:3.summary: Judges 18:19 tells the Levite, “Be silent, put your hand over your mouth”; Proverbs 30:32 warns against stretching out “your hand with fighting.” The Greek of 30:32 does not contain the instruction to cover one’s mouth.
judges-18:19:3.why: Readers should not infer a shared saying about silence from wording that is absent in this edition.
judges-18:19:3.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

judges-18:20:1.summary: Judges 18:20 says “The priest’s heart was glad” as he took the ephod and images; Proverbs 30:15 describes a leech whose daughters were never content to say “Enough!” Neither text shares wording or a stated theme of greed.
judges-18:20:1.why: Linking them requires assuming an insatiable motive the narrative does not state, so the proverb does not clarify the priest’s choice.
judges-18:20:1.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

judges-18:27:0.summary: Judges 18:27 says the Danites “struck them with the edge of the sword” at Laish; Joshua 19:48 says “the sons of Judah … fought against Lachish, captured it, struck it with the edge of the sword.” The wording is shared, but this edition names Judah and Lachish, not Dan and Laish.
judges-18:27:0.why: The capture is the Greek counterpart of the conquest in Judges 18, but the different names should be noted before treating them as one event.
judges-18:27:0.note: Corrected reading: English Joshua 19:47 corresponds to Joshua 19:47a–48 in the Saints Greek; Joshua 19:47 there is the inheritance summary (English 19:48).

judges-18:29:0.summary: Judges 18:29 renames Laish: “They called the city Dan”; Joshua 19:48 also ends with a renaming: “They called its name Lasendak.” The cities and names differ in this edition.
judges-18:29:0.why: Both close a conquest by renaming the captured city, but the Greek wording does not identify the two.
judges-18:29:0.note: Corrected reading: English Joshua 19:47 corresponds to Joshua 19:47a–48 in the Saints Greek; Joshua 19:47 there is the inheritance summary (English 19:48).

judges-19:16:10.summary: Judges 19:16 notes an old man coming “from his work in the field” at evening; Proverbs 24:27 says “make yourself ready for the field.” The word “field” is incidental to Judges' narrative.
judges-19:16:10.why: A passing mention of field work in a story does not illustrate the proverb's counsel on preparing before building.
judges-19:16:10.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

judges-5:24:4.summary: Judges 5:24 says “Blessed among women be Jael”; Proverbs 31:31 says, “Give her from the fruits of her hands, and let her husband be praised in the gates.” Both honor a woman, but in the Greek the public praise in 31:31 goes to her husband.
judges-5:24:4.why: The link is limited to the general theme of honoring a woman for her deeds.
judges-5:24:4.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

lamentations-5:8:2.summary: Lamentations 5:8 mourns that “slaves ruled over us”; Proverbs 30:22 counts “a household servant becomes king” among things the earth cannot bear. Both describe servants ruling as a disorder and a burden.
lamentations-5:8:2.why: The proverb names in general terms the humiliation Lamentations describes from experience.
lamentations-5:8:2.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

leviticus-11:5:1.summary: Leviticus 11:5 in the Saints text names “the hare” as unclean; Proverbs 30:26 speaks of “the rock badgers.” The animal that links these verses in Hebrew-based translations does not appear in the Greek of Leviticus 11:5.
leviticus-11:5:1.why: With different animals named, the food law and the proverb share no subject in this edition.
leviticus-11:5:1.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

leviticus-11:15:3.summary: Leviticus 11:15 lists “the raven and those like it” among unclean birds; Proverbs 30:17 says “ravens from the ravines” will peck out the mocking eye. The raven is mentioned for different purposes in each.
leviticus-11:15:3.why: A shared bird name in a food law does not help interpret the proverb.
leviticus-11:15:3.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

leviticus-19:3:4.summary: Leviticus 19:3 commands, “Each shall revere his father and his mother”; Proverbs 30:17 curses an eye “mocking a father and dishonoring a mother’s old age.” The proverb pictures the opposite of the reverence the Law requires.
leviticus-19:3:4.why: Proverbs 30:17 shows what is at stake in the Law's command to revere both parents.
leviticus-19:3:4.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

leviticus-19:15:2.summary: Leviticus 19:15 forbids injustice “in judgment,” whether favoring “the person of the poor” or admiring “the person of the mighty”; Proverbs 24:23 says “to show deference to a face in judgment is not good.”
leviticus-19:15:2.why: The proverb repeats the law’s ban on partiality toward any person in court, rich or poor.
leviticus-19:15:2.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

leviticus-20:9:5.summary: Leviticus 20:9 says “Any man who speaks evil of his father or his mother shall surely be put to death”; Proverbs 30:17 curses “an eye mocking a father and dishonoring a mother.” Both pronounce death on contempt toward parents.
leviticus-20:9:5.why: The proverb's curse echoes the Law's penalty for speaking evil of parents.
leviticus-20:9:5.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

leviticus-24:6:6.summary: Leviticus 24:6 sets the loaves in two rows “on the pure table before the Lord”; Exodus 39:17 lists “the table of presentation and all its utensils, and the bread of the Presence.”
leviticus-24:6:6.why: It links the table and bread made for the tabernacle with the law for arranging the loaves on it.
leviticus-24:6:6.note: Corrected reading: English Exodus 39:36 (the table and showbread) is Exodus 39:17 in the Saints Greek order; it was previously shown as 39:15 (the altar).

leviticus-5:21:3.summary: Leviticus 5:21 addresses one who “deals falsely with his neighbour” over a deposit or partnership; Proverbs 24:28 says “Do not be a false witness against your fellow citizen.” Both forbid dishonesty toward a neighbor, but Leviticus concerns fraud, not testimony.
leviticus-5:21:3.why: The pairing shows a broad ethic of honesty toward one's neighbor rather than a shared teaching on witness.
leviticus-5:21:3.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

leviticus-8:2:1.summary: Leviticus 8:2 tells Moses to take “Aaron and his sons, his robes, the anointing oil”; Exodus 39:18 lists “Aaron’s robes for the sanctuary and his sons’ robes for priestly service.”
leviticus-8:2:1.why: The robes completed in Exodus are the ones used at the ordination of Aaron and his sons.
leviticus-8:2:1.note: Corrected reading: English Exodus 39:41 (the priestly garments) is Exodus 39:18 in the Saints Greek order; it was previously shown as 39:21 (the pegs).

luke-1:28:9.summary: Luke 1:28 greets Mary, “Rejoice, you who have been favoured!”; Proverbs 31:29–30 says “you stand above and have surpassed them all” and “an understanding woman is blessed.” Both single out a woman as favored, but share no specific wording.
luke-1:28:9.why: The link is a broad likeness between two women singled out for honor.
luke-1:28:9.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

luke-12:35:8.summary: Luke 12:35 says, “Let your loins be girded”; Proverbs 31:17 says, “Having girded her waist strongly, she braced her arms for work.”
luke-12:35:8.why: Both use girding as the image of readiness for work, which shows how familiar the picture was behind Jesus’ call to watchfulness.
luke-12:35:8.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

luke-14:28:0.summary: Luke 14:28 asks who, “wanting to build a tower,” does not “first sit down and calculate the expense”; Proverbs 24:27 says “Prepare your works … make yourself ready for the field,” and then “you will rebuild your house.” Both teach preparing beforehand as the condition for building.
luke-14:28:0.why: Proverbs supplies an older wisdom form of the prudence Jesus uses as an image for counting the cost of discipleship.
luke-14:28:0.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

luke-16:3:7.summary: Luke 16:3 records the steward saying “I am not strong enough to dig; I am ashamed to beg” as he loses his post; Proverbs 24:30–34 warns that dozing and neglect bring poverty. The steward is not described as dozing or neglecting a field, so the passages share neither wording nor situation.
luke-16:3:7.why: Reading the steward’s dilemma as laziness goes beyond either text, so the link does not clarify the parable.
luke-16:3:7.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

malachi-1:6:9.summary: Malachi 1:6 begins, “A son honors his father,” and asks, “If I am a father, where is My honor?”; Proverbs 30:17 curses an eye “mocking a father.” Honor owed to a father is shared, but Malachi applies it to the priests' contempt for God.
malachi-1:6:9.why: The link rests on a general principle of honoring fathers rather than a shared teaching.
malachi-1:6:9.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

malachi-2:14:10.summary: In Malachi 2:14 the people ask “For what reason?” though they abandoned “the wife of your youth”; Proverbs 30:20 describes one who “says she has done nothing improper.” Both involve marital unfaithfulness met with professed innocence.
malachi-2:14:10.why: The proverb gives a parallel picture of feigned innocence, though Malachi speaks of men abandoning wives, not of adultery concealed by washing.
malachi-2:14:10.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

mark-13:36:6.summary: Mark 13:36 warns that the master “may come suddenly and find you sleeping”; Proverbs 24:33–34 warns that while one sleeps, want comes “like a good runner.” Both picture something arriving swiftly on a sleeper, but Mark speaks of readiness for the master’s return and Proverbs of poverty.
mark-13:36:6.why: The common image of being overtaken while asleep is suggestive but the subjects differ.
mark-13:36:6.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

mark-7:10:6.summary: Mark 7:10 cites Moses, “Honor your father and your mother,” and “Let whoever speaks evil of father or mother surely die”; Proverbs 30:17 curses “an eye mocking a father and dishonoring a mother.” Both treat contempt for parents as deserving death.
mark-7:10:6.why: Jesus' appeal to the Law on honoring parents matches the proverb's severe judgment.
mark-7:10:6.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

matthew-15:4:13.summary: Matthew 15:4 cites “Honor father and mother” and “Whoever reviles father or mother must surely die”; Proverbs 30:17 curses “an eye mocking a father and dishonoring a mother.” Both condemn contempt for both parents with a death sentence.
matthew-15:4:13.why: The proverb reinforces the commandment Jesus says the tradition had evaded.
matthew-15:4:13.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

matthew-19:19:8.summary: Matthew 19:19 lists “honor father and mother” among the commandments; Proverbs 30:17 curses an eye “dishonoring a mother’s old age.” The proverb describes the breach of the command Jesus cites.
matthew-19:19:8.why: It connects the commandment to the proverb's picture of its violation.
matthew-19:19:8.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

matthew-26:25:7.summary: In Matthew 26:25 Judas asks, “Surely it is not I, Rabbi?”; Proverbs 30:20 describes one who “says she has done nothing improper.” Both show a guilty person disowning wrongdoing.
matthew-26:25:7.why: The link is a general pattern of denial; the betrayal and the proverb’s adultery are different matters.
