matthew-26:25:7.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

micah-5:4:14.summary: Micah 5:4 promises “seven shepherds and eight bites of people”; Proverbs 30:18 begins, “Three things are impossible for me to understand, and the fourth.” Both use the rising-number pattern, but nothing else.
micah-5:4:14.why: The pairing illustrates a shared literary device, not a shared subject.
micah-5:4:14.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

micah-5:4:24.summary: Micah 5:4 promises “seven shepherds and eight” to rise against Assyria; Proverbs 30:29 begins “three things go on their way well, and the fourth.” The only link is the rising numerical pattern; the subjects are unrelated.
micah-5:4:24.why: It illustrates a shared literary device, not a shared meaning.
micah-5:4:24.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

micah-7:6:18.summary: Micah 7:6 laments that “a son dishonors his father, a daughter will rise against her mother”; Proverbs 30:17 curses “an eye mocking a father and dishonoring a mother’s old age.” Both describe children turning in contempt against both parents.
micah-7:6:18.why: Micah shows as a mark of social collapse the dishonor Proverbs 30:17 curses.
micah-7:6:18.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

micah-7:13:10.summary: Micah 7:13 says the land will be ruined “from the fruits of their practices”; Proverbs 31:31 says, “Give her from the fruits of her hands.” Both use the idea of fruits of one's deeds, for judgment in Micah and reward in Proverbs.
micah-7:13:10.why: The shared phrase gives only a loose contrast between deeds bringing ruin and deeds bringing reward.
micah-7:13:10.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

nehemiah-2:10:15.summary: Nehemiah 2:10 names “Tobia the Ammoni servant” among those displeased by Nehemiah’s arrival; Proverbs 30:22 speaks of “a household servant” who “becomes king.” The word servant is the only link, and Nehemiah does not describe Tobia ruling.
nehemiah-2:10:15.why: The shared word does not establish a real connection.
nehemiah-2:10:15.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

nehemiah-5:9:6.summary: Nehemiah 5:9 rebukes the nobles, “What you are doing is not good,” over their treatment of fellow Jews; Proverbs 24:23 concerns deference “in judgment.” The only common element is the phrase “not good.”
nehemiah-5:9:6.why: Nehemiah addresses exploitation and reproach before the nations, not partiality in judging, so the link does not inform either verse.
nehemiah-5:9:6.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

numbers-12:11:2.summary: In Numbers 12:11 Aaron pleads, “we acted ignorantly in that we sinned”; Proverbs 30:32 warns that giving yourself “over to merriment” and fighting brings dishonor. The Greek of 30:32 has no reference to acting foolishly, the link in Hebrew-based translations.
numbers-12:11:2.why: Aaron’s confession and the proverb’s warning share no wording or subject in the Saints text.
numbers-12:11:2.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

numbers-23:24:8.summary: Numbers 23:24 says Israel “will rise like a lion cub” and will not rest until it eats prey; Proverbs 30:30 describes “a lion’s cub, stronger than beasts, which does not turn back.” Both use the lion cub as a picture of unyielding strength.
numbers-23:24:8.why: The shared image helps show the confident, unstoppable bearing that both texts attribute to the lion cub.
numbers-23:24:8.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

numbers-4:6:6.summary: Numbers 4:6 covers the ark with “a covering of blue skin” and “a cloth entirely of blue”; Exodus 39:18 lists the priests’ robes. The passages concern different objects.
numbers-4:6:6.why: The overlap in English Bibles rests on the general word for service cloths; the Saints readings share nothing specific.
numbers-4:6:6.note: Corrected reading: English Exodus 39:41 (the priestly garments) is Exodus 39:18 in the Saints Greek order; it was previously shown as 39:21 (the pegs). Exodus 39:20 (“the coverings of blue skins”) is closer to this verse, but it is not the imported reference.

numbers-4:11:4.summary: Numbers 4:11 tells the Levites how to cover “the golden altar” for travel; Exodus 39:15 lists “the altar and all its utensils, the anointing oil, and the compounded incense” among the finished furnishings.
numbers-4:11:4.why: It connects the incense altar made for the tabernacle with the rules for carrying it.
numbers-4:11:4.note: Corrected reading: English Exodus 39:38 (the golden altar, anointing oil and incense) is Exodus 39:15 in the Saints Greek order; it was previously shown as 39:17 (the table).

numbers-4:13:2.summary: Numbers 4:13 covers the altar with “a cloth entirely of purple”; Exodus 39:18 lists “Aaron’s robes for the sanctuary and his sons’ robes.” One concerns an altar covering, the other priestly clothing.
numbers-4:13:2.why: Beyond fabric for sanctuary use, the passages share no specific object, command or wording.
numbers-4:13:2.note: Corrected reading: English Exodus 39:41 (the priestly garments) is Exodus 39:18 in the Saints Greek order; it was previously shown as 39:21 (the pegs).

numbers-5:13:2.summary: Numbers 5:13 describes a wife who has lain with another man and “conceals it, though she is defiled”; Proverbs 30:20 describes an adulterous woman who “washes herself and says she has done nothing improper.”
numbers-5:13:2.why: Both address adultery hidden from view, the case the law of Numbers 5 was given to expose.
numbers-5:13:2.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

philippians-2:20:8.summary: Philippians 2:20 says “I have no one of like mind who will sincerely care about your circumstances”; Proverbs 31:29 says “you stand above and have surpassed them all.” Paul speaks of lacking like-minded helpers, not of a woman surpassing others.
philippians-2:20:8.why: A vague sense of someone without equal is too thin to connect these verses.
philippians-2:20:8.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

philippians-4:8:32.summary: Philippians 4:8 says “if there is any praise, consider these things”; Proverbs 31:31 says “let her husband be praised in the gates.” Only the word “praise” is shared.
philippians-4:8:32.why: Paul's general list of virtues does not illuminate the proverb's closing call.
philippians-4:8:32.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

philippians-4:8:48.summary: Philippians 4:8 says “if there is any excellence and if there is any praise”; Proverbs 31:29 says “many did mighty things, but you … have surpassed them all.” The link depends on English “virtuously,” which the Saints wording does not share.
philippians-4:8:48.why: Paul's general list of virtues does not illuminate the proverb.
philippians-4:8:48.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

philippians-4:8:54.summary: Philippians 4:8 says “if there is any excellence and if there is any praise, consider these things”; Proverbs 31:10 asks, “A courageous woman—who will find her?” The link depends on English “virtuous,” which the Saints “courageous” does not share.
philippians-4:8:54.why: Paul's general list of virtues does not illuminate the proverb.
philippians-4:8:54.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

proverbs-1:8:1.summary: Proverbs 1:8 urges, “Listen, son, to your father’s discipline, and do not reject your mother’s ordinances”; Proverbs 30:17 curses an eye mocking a father and dishonoring a mother. Both address a son's stance toward both parents, one as instruction and one as warning.
proverbs-1:8:1.why: The link shows the positive counterpart to the proverb's curse, but the connection is general.
proverbs-1:8:1.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

proverbs-10:4:11.summary: Proverbs 10:4 says “poverty humbles a man, but the hands of the courageous make rich”; Proverbs 24:34 warns that “your poverty will come marching in front.” They share the word poverty, but the Greek of 10:4 does not mention slackness, so the link to the sluggard passage is looser than in Hebrew-based Bibles.
proverbs-10:4:11.why: It sets the poverty that follows dozing against the wealth of active hands, but only in general terms.
proverbs-10:4:11.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

proverbs-10:5:1.summary: Proverbs 10:5 in the Greek says “an intelligent son was preserved from scorching heat, but a lawless son is ruined by wind at harvest”; Proverbs 30:25 praises ants that “prepare their food in summer.” Hebrew-based Bibles read 10:5 as gathering in summer, but the Saints wording speaks of protection and ruin, leaving only the seasonal setting in common.
proverbs-10:5:1.why: The Greek wording removes the gathering-in-season parallel, so the link is loose.
proverbs-10:5:1.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

proverbs-10:6:4.summary: Proverbs 10:6 says “The Lord’s blessing is upon the head of the righteous”; Proverbs 24:25 says of those who reprove that “a good blessing will come upon them.”
proverbs-10:6:4.why: Both promise blessing for right conduct, but 24:25 rewards honest reproof specifically, while 10:6 speaks of the righteous in general.
proverbs-10:6:4.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

proverbs-11:16:0.summary: Proverbs 11:16 says “A gracious woman raises glory for her husband”; Proverbs 31:31 says “let her husband be praised in the gates.”
proverbs-11:16:0.why: Both show a good wife bringing honor to her husband, though 31:30 also cautions that mere “pleasing qualities are false.”
proverbs-11:16:0.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

proverbs-11:22:1.summary: Proverbs 11:22 says beauty in “a woman of bad judgment” is like “a ring in a pig’s snout”; Proverbs 31:30 says “beauty is vain” but “an understanding woman is blessed.” Both rank a woman’s judgment above her beauty, one negatively and one positively.
proverbs-11:22:1.why: The two sayings state the same value from opposite sides.
proverbs-11:22:1.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

proverbs-11:26:3.summary: Proverbs 11:26 says one who “holds grain back” may leave it “to the nations”; Proverbs 24:24 says one who calls the impious righteous will be “hated among nations.” The curse on the grain-hoarder found in Hebrew-based translations is absent from the Greek, leaving only the word “nations.”
proverbs-11:26:3.why: Hoarding grain and perverting judgment are unrelated wrongs, and without the curse wording nothing ties the verses together.
proverbs-11:26:3.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

proverbs-12:4:0.summary: Proverbs 12:4 says “A courageous woman is a crown to her husband”; Proverbs 31:10 asks, “A courageous woman—who will find her?” and 31:12 adds that “she works good things for her husband.”
proverbs-12:4:0.why: The same title, “courageous woman,” links the short proverb to the full portrait of her value to her husband.
proverbs-12:4:0.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

proverbs-12:17:3.summary: Proverbs 12:17 says “the witness of unjust people is deceitful”; Proverbs 24:28 commands, “Do not be a false witness against your fellow citizen.” Both treat deceitful testimony as a mark of the unjust.
proverbs-12:17:3.why: Proverbs 12:17 gives the observation behind the command in Proverbs 24:28.
proverbs-12:17:3.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

proverbs-12:24:12.summary: Proverbs 12:24 contrasts “the hand of chosen people” that “will rule easily” with “deceitful people” who “will become plunder”; Proverbs 24:30–34 concerns dozing and poverty. The Greek of 12:24 speaks of deceit rather than slackness, so the diligence-and-laziness link found in Hebrew-based Bibles is absent.
proverbs-12:24:12.why: In the Saints wording the verse is about deceit, not idleness, so it does not illuminate the sluggard passage.
proverbs-12:24:12.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

proverbs-13:25:8.summary: Proverbs 13:25 says “the lives of the impious are in want”; Proverbs 24:34 says “your want like a good runner.” They share the word want, but 13:25 ties want to impiety while 24:34 ties it to dozing.
proverbs-13:25:8.why: The shared word points to the general theme of lack but the causes differ.
proverbs-13:25:8.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

proverbs-14:1:0.summary: Proverbs 14:1 says “Wise women built houses”; Proverbs 31:27 says “The occupations of her houses are secure,” and 31:13 says she “made useful work with her hands.”
proverbs-14:1:0.why: The portrait in Proverbs 31 shows in detail how a wise woman builds up her house, the point 14:1 states briefly.
proverbs-14:1:0.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

proverbs-14:9:4.summary: Proverbs 14:9 says “The houses of lawless people will owe purification”; Proverbs 30:20 says an adulterous woman “washes herself.” The Greek of 14:9 lacks the mockery of sin found in Hebrew-based translations, and owing purification is not the same as the woman’s washing.
proverbs-14:9:4.why: The verses touch cleansing in different senses, so the link does not clarify either one.
proverbs-14:9:4.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

proverbs-15:20:8.summary: Proverbs 15:20 says “a foolish son sneers at his mother”; Proverbs 30:17 curses “an eye mocking a father and dishonoring a mother’s old age.” Both portray a son's scorn for his parents.
proverbs-15:20:8.why: Proverbs 15:20 names the folly whose punishment 30:17 describes.
proverbs-15:20:8.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

proverbs-15:23:5.summary: Proverbs 15:23 says the evil person will not “say anything timely and good for the community”; Proverbs 24:26 says “lips answering good words will kiss.” The Greek of 15:23 is about the evil speaker, not the joy of an apt answer.
proverbs-15:23:5.why: Read together, the verses contrast the speech of the evil person with the good answer the proverb commends, but the overlap is only “good” speech.
proverbs-15:23:5.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

proverbs-16:28:11.summary: Proverbs 16:28 says a crooked man “lights a torch of deceit” and “separates friends”; Proverbs 30:33 says that if you “drag out words, disputes and battles will come out.” Both describe conduct that produces conflict.
proverbs-16:28:11.why: The theme of stirring up strife is shared, but 16:28 speaks of deceit rather than the prolonged words of 30:33.
proverbs-16:28:11.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

proverbs-17:15:3.summary: Proverbs 17:15 condemns one “who judges the unjust righteous”; Proverbs 24:24 says one who says of the impious, “He is righteous,” will be “accursed among peoples.”
proverbs-17:15:3.why: Both condemn declaring the guilty righteous, and 24:24 adds the public curse that falls on such a judge.
proverbs-17:15:3.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

proverbs-17:19:8.summary: Greek Proverbs 17:19 reads “One who loves sin rejoices in battles”; Proverbs 24:27 concerns preparing one's work and rebuilding a house. The Hebrew line about exalting one's gate, which may have prompted the link, is absent from the Saints reading.
proverbs-17:19:8.why: In the Saints wording the two verses share no subject, so the reference does not help.
proverbs-17:19:8.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

proverbs-18:5:4.summary: Proverbs 18:5 says, “To admire the face of the impious is not good,” nor to turn aside what is just “in judgment”; Proverbs 24:23 says “to show deference to a face in judgment is not good.”
proverbs-18:5:4.why: The two proverbs share the terms “face,” “not good,” and “judgment,” and teach the same rule against partial verdicts.
proverbs-18:5:4.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

proverbs-18:9:2.summary: Proverbs 18:9 says one who “does not heal himself in his works” is “brother to one who ruins himself”; Proverbs 24:30–34 shows a neglected field going to ruin and dozing leading to poverty. Both connect neglect with self-inflicted ruin, but the Greek of 18:9 does not name laziness as Hebrew-based Bibles do.
proverbs-18:9:2.why: It loosely pairs two sayings about neglect ending in ruin.
proverbs-18:9:2.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

proverbs-18:22:1.summary: Proverbs 18:22 says “One who found a good wife found favors”; Proverbs 31:10 asks, “who will find her? Such a woman is more precious than costly stones.”
proverbs-18:22:1.why: Both speak of finding a good wife and of her great worth, and the later poem shows what that worth looks like.
proverbs-18:22:1.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

proverbs-19:10:0.summary: Proverbs 19:10 says luxury does not benefit “a fool” nor “a household servant if he begins to rule”; Proverbs 30:22 lists among things the earth cannot bear “if a household servant becomes king, and a fool is filled with food.” Both pair the servant who rules with the fool who is well supplied.
proverbs-19:10:0.why: The two proverbs share the same paired images of things out of their proper place.
proverbs-19:10:0.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

proverbs-19:14:1.summary: Proverbs 19:14 says “a wife is joined to a husband by God”; Proverbs 31:10–31 describes the worth of a “courageous woman” to her husband, ending in 31:30 with “the fear of the Lord.” The Greek of 19:14 speaks of any wife, not a prudent wife as in Hebrew-based translations.
proverbs-19:14:1.why: Both view a good marriage as coming from God, but the link is general rather than specific to the poem’s portrait.
proverbs-19:14:1.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

proverbs-19:15:5.summary: Greek Proverbs 19:15 says “the life of an idle person will hunger”; Proverbs 24:33 gives the sluggard's words, “A little I doze, a little I sleep.” The Hebrew image of slothfulness casting into deep sleep is absent from the Saints reading, leaving only the general theme of idleness.
proverbs-19:15:5.why: Both warn against idleness, but in the Greek wording no shared image of sleep ties them together.
proverbs-19:15:5.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

proverbs-19:24:3.summary: Proverbs 19:24 pictures one who “hides his hands in his lap” and will not even bring them to his mouth; Proverbs 24:33 has the idler “clasp my chest with my hands.” Both use the image of hands held idle against the body to depict self-defeating inactivity.
proverbs-19:24:3.why: The matching image of idle hands helps a reader see these as two sketches of the same character.
proverbs-19:24:3.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

proverbs-19:26:2.summary: Proverbs 19:26 says “One who dishonors a father and thrusts his mother away will be put to shame”; Proverbs 30:17 curses an eye “dishonoring a mother’s old age.” Both describe dishonor of father and mother and its consequence.
proverbs-19:26:2.why: The two proverbs together show shame and destruction as the outcome of dishonoring parents.
proverbs-19:26:2.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

proverbs-20:4:7.summary: Proverbs 20:4 describes “a lazy person” who is not ashamed and one who “borrows grain at harvest”; Proverbs 24:34 warns that idleness brings “poverty” and “want.” Both show laziness ending in need for food at the time others have plenty.
proverbs-20:4:7.why: Proverbs 20:4 gives a concrete case of the want that 24:34 predicts.
proverbs-20:4:7.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

proverbs-20:13:10.summary: Proverbs 20:13 in the Greek reads “do not love speaking against others … open your eyes and be filled with loaves”; Proverbs 24:33–34 warns that dozing brings poverty. Hebrew-based Bibles read “love not sleep,” but the Saints wording warns against slander, leaving only “open your eyes” as a faint contrast to dozing.
proverbs-20:13:10.why: The Greek wording removes most of the sleep-and-poverty parallel, so the link adds little.
proverbs-20:13:10.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

proverbs-21:25:7.summary: Proverbs 21:25 says “desires kill a lazy person, for his hands do not choose to do anything”; Proverbs 24:33–34 shows idle hands clasped to the chest and want arriving “like a good runner.” Both trace ruin to hands that refuse to work.
proverbs-21:25:7.why: Together they show laziness as a choice of the hands that leads to unmet need.
proverbs-21:25:7.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

proverbs-23:21:9.summary: Proverbs 23:21 warns that the drunkard “will become poor” and “every sleepy person” will wear rags; Proverbs 24:33–34 says “a little I sleep” leads to “your poverty.” Both make habitual sleepiness a direct path to poverty.
proverbs-23:21:9.why: The two warnings confirm each other on the cost of sleepiness.
proverbs-23:21:9.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

proverbs-23:22:1.summary: Proverbs 23:22 says “do not despise your mother because she has grown old”; Proverbs 30:17 curses an eye “dishonoring a mother’s old age.” Both single out contempt for an aging mother.
proverbs-23:22:1.why: Proverbs 30:17 states the penalty for the very contempt 23:22 forbids.
proverbs-23:22:1.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

proverbs-25:8:3.summary: Proverbs 25:8 warns, “Do not rush quickly into battle”; Proverbs 30:33 says that dragging out words makes “disputes and battles” come out. Both counsel against provoking conflict.
proverbs-25:8:3.why: The shared word “battle” and the caution against strife connect them, but each verse makes its point differently.
proverbs-25:8:3.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

proverbs-25:11:3.summary: Proverbs 25:11 compares “speaking a word” to “a golden apple on a carnelian necklace”; Proverbs 24:26 says “lips answering good words will kiss.” Both value well-spoken words through an image, but the Saints wording of 25:11 lacks any reference to a fitting or right word.
proverbs-25:11:3.why: The pairing shows two pictures of the worth of good speech, though neither verse explains the other.
proverbs-25:11:3.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

proverbs-25:18:6.summary: Proverbs 25:18 likens “a man testifying false testimony against his friend” to “a club and sword and barbed arrow”; Proverbs 24:28 forbids being “a false witness against your fellow citizen.” Both address false testimony against a neighbor.
proverbs-25:18:6.why: Proverbs 25:18 shows how destructive the false witness forbidden in 24:28 is.
proverbs-25:18:6.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

proverbs-26:8:1.summary: Proverbs 26:8 compares one who “gives glory to a fool” to binding a stone in a sling; Proverbs 30:22 counts “a fool is filled with food” among things the earth cannot bear. Both treat good things given to a fool as unfitting and harmful.
proverbs-26:8:1.why: Together they show Proverbs’ consistent warning against honoring or enriching the fool.
proverbs-26:8:1.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

proverbs-26:14:4.summary: Proverbs 26:14 compares “a lazy person on his bed” to a door turning on its hinge; Proverbs 24:33 voices the sluggard's “A little I doze, a little I sleep.” Both picture the idle person who will not leave his bed.
proverbs-26:14:4.why: Read together, the two proverbs fill out the same portrait of the lazy man lingering in sleep.
proverbs-26:14:4.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

proverbs-26:21:4.summary: Proverbs 26:21 pairs “A hearth for coals and wood for fire” with “an abusive man for the turmoil of battle”; Proverbs 30:33 pairs milk yielding butter with dragged-out words yielding “disputes and battles.”
proverbs-26:21:4.why: Both use a natural cause-and-effect image to show that provoking speech reliably produces conflict.
proverbs-26:21:4.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

proverbs-27:20:2.summary: Proverbs 27:20 says “Hades and destruction are not filled” and human eyes are “insatiable”; Proverbs 30:16 names “Hades” among things that “will certainly not say, ‘It is enough.’” Both use Hades as the type of what can never be filled.
proverbs-27:20:2.why: The two sayings share the image of insatiable Hades and apply it to human desire.
proverbs-27:20:2.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

proverbs-28:21:2.summary: Proverbs 28:21 says one who has “no respect for the faces of the righteous is not good”; Proverbs 24:23 says showing “deference to a face in judgment is not good.” The Greek wording of 28:21 condemns disregard for the righteous rather than favoritism, so the shared “faces” and “not good” point in different directions.
proverbs-28:21:2.why: Hebrew-based translations make both verses warnings against partiality, but in the Saints reading only the wording overlaps.
proverbs-28:21:2.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

proverbs-28:27:11.summary: Proverbs 28:27 says one who “turns away his eye” from the poor “will be in great difficulty”; Proverbs 24:24 concerns calling the impious “righteous.” The Greek has no curse in 28:27, so the verbal hook of Hebrew-based translations is gone.
proverbs-28:27:11.why: Neglect of the poor and corrupt judgment are different subjects, and the shared consequence is too general to help.
proverbs-28:27:11.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

proverbs-29:19:2.summary: Proverbs 29:19 says “a harsh household servant will not be disciplined by words”; Proverbs 30:22 speaks of “a household servant” who “becomes king.” They share the phrase household servant, but 29:19 concerns discipline and 30:22 a servant’s unfitting rise.
proverbs-29:19:2.why: The shared phrase invites comparison but the two sayings address different problems.
proverbs-29:19:2.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

proverbs-29:22:7.summary: Proverbs 29:22 says “A wrathful man digs up strife”; Proverbs 30:33 says “if you drag out words, disputes and battles will come out.”
proverbs-29:22:7.why: Both picture strife being drawn out of a person by provocation, making 29:22 a short form of the lesson 30:33 illustrates.
proverbs-29:22:7.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

proverbs-3:15:2.summary: Proverbs 3:15 says wisdom “is more valuable than costly stones”; Proverbs 31:10 says the courageous woman “is more precious than costly stones.” The same comparison is applied to wisdom and to the woman.
proverbs-3:15:2.why: The echo invites reading the woman of Proverbs 31 alongside the personified wisdom of the book's opening chapters.
proverbs-3:15:2.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

proverbs-30:10:2.summary: Proverbs 30:10 warns against handing a household servant “over into a master’s hands, lest he curse you”; Proverbs 24:24 says one who calls the impious righteous “will be accursed among peoples.” The only overlap is the idea of being cursed.
proverbs-30:10:2.why: The verses address different wrongs, betraying a servant and perverting judgment, so the shared curse is incidental.
proverbs-30:10:2.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

proverbs-30:11:1.summary: Proverbs 30:11 says “Evil offspring curse a father and do not bless the mother”; Proverbs 30:17 curses “an eye mocking a father and dishonoring a mother.” Both verses in the same chapter condemn children's contempt for both parents.
proverbs-30:11:1.why: Verse 17 states the fate of the generation described in 30:11.
proverbs-30:11:1.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

proverbs-5:6:3.summary: Proverbs 5:6 says “her tracks are slippery and not easy to recognize”; Proverbs 30:20 speaks of “the way of an adulterous woman” who leaves no admission of wrong. Both describe a woman’s ways that conceal their nature.
proverbs-5:6:3.why: The pairing links two portraits of evasive conduct, though 5:6 by itself does not name adultery.
proverbs-5:6:3.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

proverbs-6:6:5.summary: Proverbs 6:6 tells the sluggard “go to the ant” and become wiser; Proverbs 30:25 commends “the ants, which have no strength, yet prepare their food in summer.” Both hold up the ant as a model of wisdom.
proverbs-6:6:5.why: The two passages together show the ant as Proverbs’ standing example of foresight.
proverbs-6:6:5.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

proverbs-6:6:13.summary: Proverbs 6:6 tells the “sluggard” to “see” the ant’s ways and become wiser; in Proverbs 24:32 the speaker “looked so as to choose discipline” after observing the neglected field. Both teach the idle to learn by observation, and 24:33–34 repeats the sleep-and-poverty warning that follows the ant lesson in Proverbs 6.
proverbs-6:6:13.why: It links two Proverbs passages that address the sluggard through a lesson drawn from looking at the world.
proverbs-6:6:13.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

proverbs-6:7:1.summary: Proverbs 6:7 says the ant has “no one forcing it” and “is under no master”; Proverbs 30:27 says the locust “is without a king, yet marches out in good order.” Both commend small creatures that act wisely without a ruler.
proverbs-6:7:1.why: Together they make the same point about self-directed order in nature.
proverbs-6:7:1.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

proverbs-6:8:2.summary: Proverbs 6:8 says the ant “prepares its food in summer”; Proverbs 30:25 says the ants “prepare their food in summer.” The wording is nearly identical.
proverbs-6:8:2.why: Both describe the ant’s foresight in the same words, so each confirms the other’s point.
proverbs-6:8:2.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

proverbs-6:9:0.summary: Proverbs 6:9 asks the sluggard “when will you rise from sleep?”; Proverbs 24:33–34 gives the sleeper’s reply, “a little I sleep,” and its outcome, “your poverty will come marching in front.” Both belong to the same sluggard warning that Proverbs gives twice.
proverbs-6:9:0.why: The question in Proverbs 6 and the answer and consequence in Proverbs 24 form a parallel pair.
proverbs-6:9:0.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

proverbs-6:10:0.summary: Proverbs 6:10 reads “you sleep a little, sit a little, doze a little, and clasp your chest with your hands a little”; Proverbs 24:33 repeats it in the first person: “A little I doze, a little I sleep, a little I clasp my chest with my hands.” The two are near-identical forms of the same saying.
proverbs-6:10:0.why: Reading them together shows Proverbs repeating one warning about creeping idleness in two collections.
proverbs-6:10:0.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

proverbs-6:11:3.summary: Proverbs 6:11 says “poverty arrives beside you like an evil traveler, and want like a good runner”; Proverbs 24:34 says “your poverty will come marching in front, and your want like a good runner.” The second line is identical and the first is a close variant.

proverbs-7:7:16.summary: Proverbs 7:7 describes “a young man lacking sense” among “the foolish”; Proverbs 24:30 speaks of “a foolish man” and “a person lacking understanding.” The phrases are similar, but 7:7 concerns a youth exposed to seduction while 24:30 compares the fool to a neglected field.
proverbs-7:7:16.why: It shows a recurring Proverbs type, the person without sense, but the two passages develop different lessons.

proverbs-7:11:2.summary: Proverbs 7:11 describes a woman who is “dissolute” and whose “feet do not rest in the house”; Proverbs 31:27 says of the courageous woman, “The occupations of her houses are secure, and she did not eat idle food.”
proverbs-7:11:2.why: The two portraits stand opposite each other in Proverbs, one woman restless and away from home, the other diligent in her house.
proverbs-7:11:2.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

proverbs-7:16:4.summary: Proverbs 7:16 has the seductress spread her bed with “double-sided rugs from Egypt”; Proverbs 31:22 says the woman “made double cloaks for her husband.” Both mention double-woven textiles, but one furnishes a seduction and the other clothes a household.
proverbs-7:16:4.why: The shared textile detail could set the two women side by side, but the texts do not draw that contrast themselves.
proverbs-7:16:4.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

proverbs-9:17:3.summary: Proverbs 9:17 invites, “Taste hidden loaves with pleasure, and sweet stolen water”; Proverbs 30:20 describes an adulterous woman who “says she has done nothing improper.” The eating image that links them in Hebrew-based translations is absent from the Greek of 30:20, which speaks of washing.
proverbs-9:17:3.why: Both portray illicit pleasure treated lightly, but in the Saints wording they share no image or terms.

psalms-103:18:0.summary: Psalm 103:18 says “a rock is a refuge for rock rabbits”; Proverbs 30:26 says the rock badgers “made their own houses in rocks.”
psalms-103:18:0.why: Both observe the same small creature sheltering in rock, which the proverb uses as a lesson in wisdom despite weakness.

psalms-111:5:7.summary: Psalm 111:5 praises the man who “has compassion and lends” and manages “his words with judgment”; Proverbs 24:30–34 describes a neglected field and the poverty that follows dozing. The texts share no wording or subject.
psalms-111:5:7.why: Generosity and wise speech are unrelated to the proverb’s warning about idleness.

psalms-111:5:17.summary: Psalm 111:5 praises the man who “has compassion and lends” and will “manage his words with judgment”; Proverbs 24:27 counsels preparing work and field before rebuilding a house. The Greek “words” points to speech, not to ordering one's affairs, so the familiar English link to managing business is lost.
psalms-111:5:17.why: Generosity and careful speech are not the subject of Proverbs 24:27, so the cross-reference does not clarify either verse.
psalms-111:5:17.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

psalms-126:2:8.summary: Psalm 126:2 says “it is vain for you to rise early” and eat “bread of pain” when the Lord gives sleep; Proverbs 31:15 praises the woman who “rises in the night,” and 31:18 says “her lamp is not extinguished throughout the night.” Both speak of early rising and night labor, but the psalm calls anxious toil vain while the proverb commends diligent work.
psalms-126:2:8.why: The pairing can prompt reflection on toil and trust, though the passages make different points.

psalms-126:4:1.summary: Psalm 126:4 compares “the sons of those who have been cast out” to arrows in a mighty man’s hand; Proverbs 31:28 says the woman’s mercy raised up her children and “they became wealthy.” Apart from mentioning children, the passages are unrelated.
psalms-126:4:1.why: The general mention of children gives no specific insight into either verse.

psalms-143:12:7.summary: Psalm 143:12 prays that daughters be “beautified, adorned all around like the likeness of a sanctuary”; Proverbs 31:10–27 portrays a wife's work, trade, and care of her household. The psalm's image of blessed children does not describe such a woman.

psalms-146:11:11.summary: Psalm 146:11 says “the Lord takes pleasure in those who fear Him”; Proverbs 31:30 calls the understanding woman blessed and says “let her praise the fear of the Lord.” Both commend fearing the Lord, a common theme, without a more specific link.
psalms-146:11:11.why: The shared phrase confirms a familiar teaching but adds little to either verse.

psalms-31:5:21.summary: In Psalm 31:5 the psalmist says, “I did not cover my lawlessness” and confesses it; in Proverbs 30:20 the adulterous woman “says she has done nothing improper.”
psalms-31:5:21.why: Set side by side, confession that leads to forgiveness stands against denial that hides sin.
psalms-31:5:21.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

psalms-35:5:14.summary: Psalm 35:5 describes a wicked man who “stood by every way that was not good”; Proverbs 24:23 concerns deference “in judgment.” The phrase “not good” is the only overlap.
psalms-35:5:14.why: The psalm portrays a schemer’s habits, not partiality in judging, so the link adds nothing to either text.

romans-1:30:36.summary: Romans 1:30 includes “disobedient to parents” in a list of vices; Proverbs 30:17 curses an eye mocking a father and dishonoring a mother. Both regard wrong toward parents as sin, but Romans only names it in passing.
romans-1:30:36.why: The link is a general theme of disobedience to parents.

romans-12:11:17.summary: Romans 12:11 urges “do not be slack in zeal; be fervent in spirit”; Proverbs 24:33–34 warns that dozing brings poverty. Both oppose slackness, but Romans speaks of zeal in serving the Lord and Proverbs of material neglect.
romans-12:11:17.why: The proverb offers a concrete image of slackness, but the link is only a general theme.
romans-12:11:17.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

romans-13:4:2.summary: Romans 13:4 calls the ruling authority “an avenger who brings wrath on the one who practices evil”; Proverbs 24:23–24 forbids deference “in judgment” and calling the impious “righteous.” Both concern just judgment of wrongdoers, but only in general terms.
romans-13:4:2.why: The proverb describes the impartial justice expected of those who judge, a loose background for Paul’s view of the authorities.
romans-13:4:2.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

romans-2:11:12.summary: Romans 2:11 states, “there is no partiality with God”; Proverbs 24:23 says “to show deference to a face in judgment is not good.”
romans-2:11:12.why: The proverb asks of human judges the same impartiality Paul attributes to God’s judgment.
romans-2:11:12.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

ruth-3:11:0.summary: Ruth 3:11 says “the whole tribe of my people knows that you are a woman of strength”; Proverbs 31:29 says “many did mighty things, but you … have surpassed them all.” Both speak of a woman's recognized worth, but in the Greek 31:31 has “her husband” praised in the gates rather than the woman.

ruth-3:11:1.summary: Ruth 3:11 says “the whole tribe of my people knows that you are a woman of strength”; Proverbs 31:10 asks, “A courageous woman—who will find her?” Both describe a woman of strength and worth.
ruth-3:11:1.why: Ruth gives a named example of the woman praised in Proverbs 31:10.
ruth-3:11:1.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

ruth-4:2:0.summary: Ruth 4:2 says Boaz “took ten men from the elders of the city” and they sat down; Proverbs 31:23 says her husband “sits in council with the elder inhabitants of the land.” Both depict a man sitting with the elders in public council.
ruth-4:2:0.why: Boaz's council with the elders shows the setting in which the husband of Proverbs 31:23 is honored.
ruth-4:2:0.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

ruth-4:10:11.summary: Ruth 4:10 has Boaz declare, “I have also acquired Ruth the Moabite … as my wife”; Proverbs 31:10 asks, “A courageous woman—who will find her?” Boaz finds such a woman in Ruth, but the link relies on Ruth 3:11 rather than this verse.
ruth-4:10:11.why: The connection is narrative and indirect.
ruth-4:10:11.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

song-of-songs-6:9:5.summary: Song of Songs 6:9 calls the beloved “the only one,” whom “daughters” call blessed and queens “praise”; Proverbs 31:28–29 has “her husband praised her,” saying “many daughters” did well “but you … have surpassed them all.” Both praise a woman as surpassing all other women, using “daughters” and praise.
song-of-songs-6:9:5.why: The two passages share the form of praise that ranks one woman above all others.
song-of-songs-6:9:5.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.

song-of-songs-7:13:23.summary: Song of Songs 7:13 invites the beloved to see whether “the vine has blossomed” in “the vineyards”; Proverbs 24:30–31 likens a person lacking understanding to a vineyard that will “become wasteland.” Only the vineyard setting is shared.
song-of-songs-7:13:23.why: One passage uses a flowering vineyard for love and the other a neglected one for folly, so the shared word does not connect their meaning.
song-of-songs-7:13:23.note: Corrected reading: the Saints edition places this passage in its Greek-order section of Proverbs; it was previously reported as unavailable.
